newsitem.title: INDIA: Rival parties claim lead in India Punjab elections.
newsitem.headline: Rival parties claim lead in India Punjab elections.

text.p: The main rival political parties in India's northern state of Punjab each claimed they were leading in local polls but analysts said on Sunday that a pro-Sikh party was likely to form the new government.
Amid tight security, election officials on Sunday began counting votes at 8 a.m. (0230 GMT) across the state for the 117-seat state legislature. Results are expected to be announced by late evening.
"Counting of votes has started peacefully. There is repolling at two polling stations due to minor problems," Rajendra Singh told Reuters in Chandigarh, the state capital.
More than 65 percent of Punjab's 15 million voters turned out on Friday in a peaceful election for the state legislature that is expected to thrust the pro-Sikh Akali Dal party into power.

The polls for the state assembly were the first in almost two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence, but officials said there were too many divisions within the state's political groups to ensure badly-needed stability.
Officials said former Punjab chief minister Prakash Singh Badal's Akali Dal party has been seen as sympathetic to Sikh militants' demands for a separate homeland called Khalistan.

The Dal's poll alliance with India's main opposition group, the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), was seen as offering a chance to Punjab's two main communities -- Hindus and Sikhs -- to heal their mistrust, analysts said.
"Our estimate is that Akali Dal along with BJP is way ahead of other political parties in these elections," Sukbhir Grewal, an independent political analyst in Chandigarh, told Reuters.
"The (combination) will get 100 seats of which 15 will belong to the BJP," Kanwaljit Singh, a Akali Dal candidate from Banur constituency, and a former state minister, said.
"These elections will prove (to be a) triumph for Punjabi unity," said Balramji Das Tandon, a BJP candidate from the neighbouring Rajpura constitency.
But Raj Khurana, a Congress Party candidate and Tandon's rival candidate from Rajpura, was confident that his party would form the next government.
"I am expecting to win by 10,000 votes. We (Congress) will form the government," Khurana said.
Punjab's ruling Congress party, led by the state's first woman chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, claims credit for the virtual weeding out of Sikh militancy from the region.
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.

The showdown triggered a bloody spate of violence in the state. Then-prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what was believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
The state polls in 1992, which revived local democracy after more than a decade of separatist violence, were held in an atmosphere of fear and overbearing security.
